newsitem.title: USA: NU sees near break-even while plants closed.
newsitem.headline: NU sees near break-even while plants closed.

text.p: Northeast Utilities said Tuesday it expects to operate on a roughly break-even basis this year while the three units of the Millstone nuclear power plant are off line.

The expectation was included with the company's report it lost $76.4 million, or $0.60 per share, in the fourth quarter after a $63 million accounting reserve to help pay for 1997 spending related to the utility's nuclear program.
NU said its nuclear operation and maintenance expense in 1996, including the $63 million reserve, was about $620 million. It is expected to be about $600 million this year.
NU said the $63 million reserve includes a $23 million fourth quarter addition to the $40 million reserve taken in the third quarter.
It said higher nuclear operation and maintenance costs, including the $23 million, reduced fourth quarter earnings by $55 million, or $0.25 per share.

The utility said said December storm damage not covered by insurance reduced quarterly earnings $15 million, or $0.07 per share, and the July 1996 Connecticut rate settlement had a negative impact of $10 million, or $0.05 per share.
NU said it expects at least one Millstone unit to begin operation in the second half of 1997, but not until after the summer peak electric demand season is over.
It pointed out that none of the three Millstone units can resume operations until the Nuclear Regulatory Commission formally votes to permit restart.
Primarily because of work undertaken to return the Millstone units to service, NU said, its non-fuel operating and maintenance costs were $1.57 billion last year compared with $1.25 billion in 1995.

For the fourth quarter, it said, replacement power costs totaled $127 million, or $0.58 per share, and spending to ensure Connecticut has adequate generation capacity trimmed the quarter another $8 million, or $0.04 per share.
It said fuel and purchased power costs rose to $1.14 billion from $909 million in 1995, primarily because of the need to replace the power the three shutdown units would produce if operating.
Despite cool weather in July and warm weather in December, NU said, its retail power sales were up 1.6 percent for the year, 2.4 percent on a weather-adjusted basis.
